Frequently asked questions

Source: vignettes/articles/faq.Rmd
faq.Rmd

Short answers to questions that come up when building a media mix model or attributing conversions with mediamix. Each one names the functions and arguments involved, and their help pages have the detail. The examples use the package’s simulated data, mm_weekly and mm_events.

library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)
data(mm_events)

Carryover

Should the adstock kernel be normalised?

By default (normalise = TRUE) the kernel’s weights sum to 1, so a steady spend of 100 a week adstocks to 100 once the filter has filled, and a coefficient on the adstocked column reads per unit of spend. With normalise = FALSE, the convention Robyn uses, the same spend accumulates to 100 / (1 - decay), and the coefficient reads per unit of accumulated media. The two series differ only by a constant factor, so in a least-squares fit only the coefficient’s scale changes. A saturation half_max given as an amount belongs to one convention and is wrong for the other, while one set relative to the series’ own reference level, as step_saturation() sets it, gives the same curve under both. Keep one convention for a project, and compare coefficients only between models fitted the same way.

steady <- rep(100, 100)
c(normalised = tail(adstock_geometric(steady, decay = 0.8), 1),
  raw = tail(adstock_geometric(steady, decay = 0.8, normalise = FALSE), 1))
#> normalised        raw 
#>        100        500

Why are the first weeks of an adstocked series low?

Every filter starts from zero unless told otherwise, as if nothing had been spent before the first row. A slow channel takes weeks to fill: at a decay of 0.85 a steady spend reaches 15% of its level in the first week, and 90% only after effective_window(0.85), 15 weeks. With spend from before the series, pass adstock_state() of it as state; without it, adstock_steady_state() gives the state that steady spend at the series’ early average would have left. warm_start = TRUE in the tuners and start = "steady" in step_adstock() apply the same correction. Robyn’s remedy, adstocking every row and fitting the model on the later rows only, works here too.

x <- rep(100, 6)
rbind(cold = adstock_geometric(x, decay = 0.85),
      steady = adstock_geometric(x, decay = 0.85,
                                 state = adstock_steady_state(x, decay = 0.85)))
#>        [,1]   [,2]   [,3]  [,4]   [,5]   [,6]
#> cold     15  27.75  38.59  47.8  55.63  62.29
#> steady  100 100.00 100.00 100.0 100.00 100.00

How long should max_lag be?

The default, max_lag = Inf, runs the geometric kernel as a recursive filter and never truncates it, so there is nothing to choose. A finite kernel should keep most of the effect: effective_window(decay, coverage) is the smallest number of periods that holds coverage of a geometric kernel’s total weight. The same number checks a fitted decay, since an effective window that approaches the length of the series is not identified by the data. The Weibull and delayed kernels have no recursive form and always need a finite max_lag; effective_window() of a comparable geometric decay is a starting point.

effective_window(c(tv = 0.85, search = 0.15), coverage = 0.9)
#>     tv search 
#>     15      2
effective_window(0.85, coverage = 0.99)
#> [1] 29

How do I convert a half-life between daily and weekly data?

decay_from_half_life() and half_life() take period, the spacing between rows in the unit the half-life is stated in. A 21-day half-life on weekly data is decay_from_half_life(21, period = 7), the same decay as a three-week half-life, and half_life(decay, period = 7) gives a weekly decay’s half-life in days. To move a decay fitted on daily data to weekly data, go through its half-life:

daily <- 0.9
days <- half_life(daily)
c(days = days, weekly = decay_from_half_life(days, period = 7),
  daily_to_the_7th = daily^7)
#>             days           weekly daily_to_the_7th 
#>           6.5788           0.4783           0.4783

The half-life is kept and the decay per row changes. Adstocking weekly totals is still not the same as adstocking daily spend and summing it to weeks, because the timing of spend within each week is lost.

How do I choose the decay?

Choose it against the KPI, by cross-validation. tune_carryover() scores each candidate (max_lag, decay) for one channel by how well a model fitted on the adstocked media predicts held-out KPI, on forward-only splits, with trend, price and seasonality passed as controls. tune_carryover_joint() does the same for every channel inside one model, so no channel is credited with another’s effect, and plot() on either result shows how sharply the data identifies each decay. To tune carryover together with saturation and a model penalty, use step_adstock_channels() or step_adstock() with step_saturation() and tune() in a tidymodels workflow, as vignette("tidymodels") shows; that search needs the tune, parsnip, workflows and yardstick packages.

What is the difference between best and best_1se?

best is the candidate with the lowest cross-validated error. best_1se is the shortest carryover (lowest half-life, then shortest kernel) whose error is within one standard error of best’s, the one-standard-error rule of Breiman et al. (1984) and Hastie et al. (2009), with the standard error taken from the paired difference between the two over the same splits. Carryover is often weakly identified, so the two can differ widely, and when they do the data cannot tell them apart. The shorter one is the more cautious claim about how long a channel keeps working, though not for every decision, since it also lowers the channel’s marginal return. In tune_carryover_joint() the rule is applied channel by channel, and best_1se_metric scores the resulting set as a whole.

set.seed(42)
spend <- pmax(0, rnorm(120, 500, 250))
kpi <- 200 + 0.5 * adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.7) + rnorm(120, sd = 60)
tuned <- tune_carryover(spend, kpi, decays = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1))
rbind(best = tuned$best, one_se = tuned$best_1se)
#>        max_lag decay half_life metric std_err n_splits
#> best       Inf   0.8     3.106  54.75   4.548       60
#> one_se     Inf   0.6     1.357  56.31   5.219       60

The true decay here is 0.7, and the noise leaves the data unable to separate 0.6 from 0.8.

How do I adstock several geographies?

Pass the geography as by. Each group is filtered on its own, so carryover never runs from the last week of one geography into the first week of the next, and each group’s rows must be in time order, since the transforms have no time index. media_transform(), transform_plan(), marginal_roi(), simulate_plan() and allocate_budget() take by too, the tuners take by with index, and step_adstock() takes by and sorts by its own index. Do not rely on dplyr::group_by() instead: the grouping does not survive into every place the transforms run, such as a recipe’s bake(), and diagnose_media() ignores it with a message naming the by to pass.

spend <- c(100, 0, 0, 200, 0, 0)
geo <- rep(c("north", "south"), each = 3)
rbind(pooled = adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.5),
      by_geo = adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.5, by = geo))
#>        [,1] [,2] [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6]
#> pooled   50   25 12.5 106.2 53.12 26.56
#> by_geo   50   25 12.5 100.0 50.00 25.00

What happens when weeks are missing?

The transforms treat adjacent rows as adjacent periods. A missing week lets the decay act once across what were two weeks, a repeated week is carried over twice, and a row out of order mixes later spend into earlier weeks, and none of these raises an error. Given the time column as date, diagnose_media() counts each of them per series in its dates table and lists them in flags, and step_adstock() warns at prep() when its index is unevenly spaced and stops on a repeated time point. Add a row for every missing period before transforming, with zero spend where the channel did not run. A missing value in a row that exists is an error in the adstock functions by default; na_action = "zero" reads it as no spend, and step_adstock() does that by default.

gappy <- mm_weekly[-10, ]   # drops one week of north
diagnose_media(gappy, media = "tv", by = "geo", date = "date")$dates
#>     group rows      start        end period out_of_order duplicated missing
#> 1   north  155 2023-01-02 2025-12-22      7            0          0       1
#> 2 central  156 2023-01-02 2025-12-22      7            0          0       0
#> 3   south  156 2023-01-02 2025-12-22      7            0          0       0
#>   irregular
#> 1         1
#> 2         0
#> 3         0

Saturation

Does saturation go before or after adstock?

Saturation goes after adstock. A saturation curve caps what the media pressure in a period can achieve, and that pressure includes carryover from earlier weeks. Saturating first puts each week’s spend through the curve on its own, so carryover never counts towards saturation, and with normalise = FALSE the carried-over values can add up past the ceiling. media_transform() adstocks first by default and warns when asked for order = "saturate_then_adstock", and in a recipe step_saturation() goes after step_adstock(). Robyn uses the same order.

Why is half_max a fraction in step_saturation()?

In saturate_hill() and media_transform(), half_max is an amount of adstocked media, the level at which the response reaches half its ceiling, so it depends on each channel’s scale. step_saturation() takes it as a fraction of each column’s reference level in the training data, its largest value by default (ref = "max"), so one tunable value means the same thing for every channel. A half_max of 0.4 there puts the half-way point at 40% of the largest adstocked value seen in training, and with by each geography gets a reference of its own.

Reporting

What does “(baseline)” mean?

contributions() gives each channel its coefficient times its transformed column, period by period, and pools everything else the model predicts into a channel called "(baseline)": the intercept, trend, price, seasonality, holidays and any other control. It is the model’s prediction minus the media effect, which is what makes each period’s contributions sum to the prediction. It holds whatever this decomposition does not attribute to media, and reporting it as organic demand overstates what the model knows. For periods the model was not fitted on, pass newdata so that the baseline comes from predict(); for a bare coefficient vector it is the intercept alone.

north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]], shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
media <- transform_plan(north, spec)
media$week <- seq_len(nrow(media))
fit <- lm(revenue ~ tv + video + search + social + display + week + price +
            seasonality + holiday, data = media)

contrib <- contributions(media[channels], fit, index = media$date)
round(tapply(contrib$contribution, contrib$channel, sum))
#> (baseline)    display     search     social         tv      video 
#>    3190425      40853     208307     132709     349629     102461

Should I use roi(), marginal_roi() or mroi()?

roi() is the average return, each channel’s total contribution divided by its total spend, which scores the period as a whole. marginal_roi() is the return on the next unit of spend. It re-runs carryover and saturation on a budget 1% larger (lift = 0.01) and divides the extra response by the extra spend, following Jin et al. (2017), so it is the one to use when moving budget. mroi() is the slope of a saturation curve at one level of transformed media, a property of the curve rather than a return on spend. Under a concave curve the marginal return is below the average one everywhere; under an S-shaped curve, below its inflection point, it can be above.

marginal_roi(north, coef(fit), spec = spec)
#>   channel  spend contribution   roi   mroi
#> 1      tv 266978       349629 1.310 1.2534
#> 2   video  53248       102461 1.924 1.1961
#> 3  search  74560       208307 2.794 1.3490
#> 4  social  36716       132709 3.614 2.0892
#> 5 display  26937        40853 1.517 0.9324

The roi column is the average return that roi() reports from these contributions, and mroi the marginal return beside it.

Why does marginal_roi() stop counting at the last week?

By default (extend = 0) it sums response over the observed weeks only, the weeks contributions() and roi() cover, so that its average return matches theirs. The carryover of spend near the end of the data then falls outside the sum, which understates the marginal return of slow channels. For a budget decision, pass extend = effective_window(decay, 0.99), which appends that many weeks of zero spend so the late carryover plays out.

tv_mroi <- function(extend) {
  marginal_roi(north$tv, coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
               adstock = spec$tv$adstock, saturation = spec$tv$saturation,
               extend = extend)$mroi
}
c(observed_weeks = tv_mroi(0),
  with_run_out = tv_mroi(effective_window(truth$decay[["tv"]], 0.99)))
#> observed_weeks   with_run_out 
#>          1.253          1.305

How do I report by geography or by year?

Give contributions() the grouping as by, and pass the same grouping to roi(), which then returns one row per channel per group. For one year or quarter of a longer decomposition, give roi() the period of each row of spend as index and the periods to keep as periods. rows in marginal_roi() raises spend only inside a planning window, and simulate_plan() and allocate_budget() take by for a panel.

year <- format(media$date, "%Y")
by_year <- contributions(media[channels], fit, index = media$date, by = year)
roi(by_year, north[channels], by = year)
#>    group channel contribution spend   roi
#> 1   2023  social        41852 11341 3.690
#> 2   2023  search        69308 24754 2.800
#> 3   2023   video        34499 19144 1.802
#> 4   2023 display        12225  8055 1.518
#> 5   2023      tv       113146 93732 1.207
#> 6   2024  social        48681 14037 3.468
#> 7   2024  search        71023 25540 2.781
#> 8   2024   video        34586 17499 1.976
#> 9   2024 display        14456  9626 1.502
#> 10  2024      tv       112666 77978 1.445
#> 11  2025  social        42177 11338 3.720
#> 12  2025  search        67976 24266 2.801
#> 13  2025   video        33376 16605 2.010
#> 14  2025 display        14172  9256 1.531
#> 15  2025      tv       123817 95268 1.300

Where do intervals come from, and what do they leave out?

block_bootstrap() puts percentile intervals on any statistic computed from a weekly table, such as coefficients, contributions or returns. It resamples blocks of consecutive weeks, so the autocorrelation that carryover creates survives (Künsch, 1989), then refits and recomputes through your statistic function. Transform the media first and put the transformed columns in the data, so that no block carries spend across a join. The intervals cover sampling variation given the model and its transform parameters; they leave out the uncertainty in choosing those parameters and any error in the specification, and on short series they cover less than their nominal level, so read them as a lower bound. Make blocks at least as long as the longest channel’s effective_window(), and for a panel pass by, so that every geography takes the same blocks of weeks.

Budgets

How do I compare plans or split a budget?

simulate_plan() runs each channel of a spend plan through its transform and coefficient, and with baseline it reports each channel’s change against another plan. reallocate() builds such a plan by moving an amount from one channel to another, and allocate_budget() splits a total across channels to maximise the predicted response within lower and upper bounds, searching a grid of steps increments so that S-shaped curves do not trap it. Both keep each channel’s weekly pattern and change only its level, so neither can start a channel that has no spend until it is given small weights in the weeks it should run; to try a different timing, build the plan yourself and pass it to simulate_plan(). The answers are only as good as the fitted curves, which are identified only over the spend levels in the data, so a move far beyond them is extrapolation and worth testing before it is made.

allocate_budget(north, spec, coef(fit), steps = 100)
#> 
#> ── Budget allocation
#> A total of 458,439, in 100 increments of 4,584.39.
#> Predicted media response: 833,959 now, 845,422 recommended.
#>  channel current_spend recommended_spend current_response recommended_response
#>       tv        266978            252141           349629               330634
#>    video         53248             45844           102461                93095
#>   search         74560             77935           208307               212779
#>   social         36716             64181           132709               177194
#>  display         26937             18338            40853                31719
#>   mroi
#>  1.299
#>  1.329
#>  1.289
#>  1.250
#>  1.203
#> The recommended plan is in $plan.

Attribution

Why do the attribution rules disagree?

Each rule is a convention for dividing a conversion among the touches before it, and the conventions favour different positions: first-touch credits the channels that open journeys and last-touch those that close them. attribute() runs all six rules on the same journeys, attribution_spread() reports each channel’s lowest and highest share, and channel_positions() shows which channels open or close journeys. A wide spread is itself the finding, since it measures how much of a channel’s credit comes from the choice of rule rather than from the data.

paths <- build_paths(mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
                     timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion")
spread <- attribution_spread(attribute(paths))
spread[, c("channel", "min_share", "max_share", "first_last_ratio")]
#>           channel min_share max_share first_last_ratio
#> 1         display   0.07187   0.29113           4.0508
#> 2     paid_search   0.09157   0.27253           0.3360
#> 3           email   0.05655   0.18314           0.3088
#> 4          social   0.11638   0.22072           1.8966
#> 5  organic_search   0.12623   0.17877           0.7061
#> 6       affiliate   0.08063   0.11711           1.4525
#> 7          direct   0.02225   0.02683           1.0492
#> 8         (blank)   0.02955   0.03379           0.9419
#> 9          (none)   0.02736   0.02982           1.0133
#> 10      (missing)   0.01569   0.01637           1.0233

Can I attribute by segment, with intervals?

Yes. Carry the segment column into the journeys with the keep argument of build_paths(), give each journey a single value, and pass the column to attribute() as by; every rule, the Markov chain included, then runs on each segment’s journeys alone. With times (and seed), attribute() adds percentile intervals by resampling journeys with replacement. The intervals show how far the shares move with the sample of journeys, with the journey construction and each rule held fixed; they say nothing about the choice of rule, which attribution_spread() measures.

Can I fit higher-order Markov chains?

markov_removal() fits the first-order chain, following Anderl et al. (2016). For higher orders, export the journeys with as_channel_paths() and pass them to ChannelAttribution::markov_model() with its order argument and the same sep on both sides; ChannelAttribution::choose_order() suggests an order. That needs the ChannelAttribution package, which mediamix suggests but does not require. For order 1 the two packages implement the same removal-effect definition, ChannelAttribution by simulation.

ca <- as_channel_paths(paths, sep = ">")
ChannelAttribution::markov_model(ca, var_path = "path",
                                 var_conv = "total_conversions",
                                 var_null = "total_null", order = 2, sep = ">")

Why keep the journeys that did not convert?

Markov removal effects compare the chance of reaching a conversion with the chance of reaching nothing, and the journeys that ended in nothing are the only evidence of the second. Without them the baseline conversion probability is 1, and every removal effect moves, up or down depending on how the dropped journeys differed from the converting ones. build_paths() keeps them by default (keep_null_paths = TRUE), as_channel_paths() counts them in total_null, and markov_removal() warns when a table has none.

How do I choose a lookback window?

Read it off your own journeys. conversion_lag() reports quantiles of the time from first touch to conversion, so a lookback at its 90% point leaves nine in ten converting journeys whole. Run it on journeys built without lookback, since a lookback caps every lag it measures, and read the lags in the journey table’s units, days by default.

conversion_lag(paths)
#>   quantile    lag
#> 1     0.50  4.535
#> 2     0.75  8.793
#> 3     0.90 13.492
#> 4     0.95 16.851
#> 5     0.99 23.538
#> 6     1.00 43.165

Other tools

Can I use the transforms with brms, Stan or glmnet?

Yes, with the transform parameters fixed before the fit. The transforms are R functions on numeric vectors, so media_transform() or transform_plan() produces columns that any model can take. contributions() reads coefficients through coef(), which serves lm(), glm() and the fixed effects of nlme and lme4; for glmnet, brms or Stan, pass the point estimates as a named vector, naming the intercept "(Intercept)" or giving it as intercept, and the baseline is then that intercept alone. marginal_roi(), simulate_plan() and allocate_budget() take coefficients as a named vector in any case. To estimate a decay or a half_max inside a Bayesian model, the transform has to be written in that model’s own language, Stan for brms.

# A ridge regression at a fixed penalty, chosen for illustration
X <- as.matrix(media[c(channels, "week", "price", "seasonality", "holiday")])
ridge <- glmnet::glmnet(X, media$revenue, alpha = 0, lambda = 50)
b <- as.matrix(coef(ridge))[, 1]
marginal_roi(north, b, spec = spec)
#>   channel  spend contribution   roi  mroi
#> 1      tv 266978       347225 1.301 1.245
#> 2   video  53248       101660 1.909 1.187
#> 3  search  74560       204208 2.739 1.322
#> 4  social  36716       126887 3.456 1.998
#> 5 display  26937        43968 1.632 1.003

Can I reproduce Robyn’s transforms?

Yes, for geometric and Weibull CDF adstock with Hill saturation. Given the series Robyn transformed and its modelling window, from_robyn() converts one channel’s theta (or shape and scale), alpha and gamma into the adstock and saturation lists that media_transform() takes, and the result matches Robyn’s series. Set inflexion = "range" for a model fitted by Robyn 3.7.0 to 3.11.1, which placed the Hill inflexion point differently. Robyn’s Weibull PDF has no exact equivalent and is refused. Migrating from Robyn works through an example.

Is any of this causal?

No. A media mix model fitted to observational data is identified only as well as its specification and the variation in the data allow, and cross-validation shows predictive value, not a causal mechanism. Attribution rules, Markov removal effects included, divide observed conversions by a convention and cannot say what would have happened without a channel. Randomised experiments, such as geo tests for media and holdouts for digital channels, measure that, and they are the way to check or calibrate a model; mediamix has no calibration step of its own. reallocate() with by sets up a move in one region, the plan for such a test.

Breiman, L., Friedman, J., Olshen, R. and Stone, C. (1984). Classification and Regression Trees. Wadsworth. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315139470

Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R. and Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-84858-7

Jin, Y., Wang, Y., Sun, Y., Chan, D. and Koehler, J. (2017). Bayesian methods for media mix modeling with carryover and shape effects. Google Inc. https://research.google/pubs/pub46001/
